doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Forming the Hamilton band with Jack Kelly and others
summary: Beginning with Jack Kelly in the ELS basement, he assembled a six-piece college band with Beldock, Fell, Krompart and others and played local gigs.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: know. We thought we were playing the blues, God knows it was terrible. But then I began to meet guys around the campus who were interested in jazz because you’d be drawn together with people like that just by chance and by the next year we had a little band: Mike Beldock on drums — Mike went on to be an important defense attorney. He was the one who got Hurricane Carter out of jail — Myron Beldock. And his partner, Elliot Abrams is a big music lawyer — not Elliot Abrams, Elliot Hoffman was a big music lawyer who represented George Wein, represented the Newport Jazz Festival, represented Dizzy, Jimmy Rushing and so forth. So they had kind of a little jazz law firm there. And John Fell was a clarinet player and John went on to be an important authority on film, particularly early film, and was head of the film department at San Francisco State. And Pete Zeeveldt, when we first met him he was a year or two behind us, Pete could only play in C but we made him move over a little bit so we had — and then the key figure was Bob Krompart. Bob is quite a good trumpet player for what he was, for a college. And his dad had been a musician and played with The Buffalodians, which was the band from Buffalo that Harold Arlen had started out in. And so — and Bob could play pretty well. I have records, I have a couple of home made records that we made of this. And we had a bass player very briefly but Wally Alpren, who went on to become a federal judge, was guitar player. And so there were six of us: myself, John — yeah that was it. That was the group. And we practiced every week. We had a weekly practice. And then we played fraternity parties, we did get some gigs off campus. I know we played Union from time to time, a couple of times anyway, we played at Colgate, I don’t know how often, we played at Wells, we played at RPI, I think we played at Ithaca College maybe, I’m not sure. But we were playing around a little bit. I think we got five bucks a man then. But it wasn’t a very good band.
It was a lot of fun I’ll bet.
It was a lot of fun. It was something that we did and something that we wanted to do.
